mainTopic: The worker's right to eat: the היקש between worker and animal, the limits learned from 'threshing' (דיש), including the cutoffs of מעשר and חלה, and whether he may singe produce before eating
overview: The גמרא asks why the תורה wrote the word 'ox' (שור) in the law against muzzling, since all animals are already included. It answers that the word links the person who muzzles to the muzzled animal, so each one may eat from both attached and detached produce. Then a series of ברייתות learn limits on a worker's eating from the word 'threshing' (דיש). He eats only from things that grow from the ground, so milking and making cheese are excluded. He eats only at the finishing stage of the work, so a weeder of garlic and onions is excluded. He eats only before the produce is finished for מעשר, and רב פפא explains that a ברייתא allowing a separator of dates to eat speaks about unripe dates. A last ברייתא uses חלה as the cutoff, and after two answers fail, רבינא joins the מעשר and חלה ברייתות into one teaching. Finally the גמרא asks whether a worker may singe produce in fire before eating it. It begins to answer from a ברייתא that lets workers dip their bread in brine so they will eat more grapes, and the discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Why does the verse say 'ox'?
steps.stepSummary: The law of muzzling covers all animals, because of a גזירה שוה with שבת. So why does the תורה specifically write 'ox'?
steps.simpleTranslation: Think about it: every kind of animal is included in the law of muzzling, because we learn 'ox' here from 'ox' in the laws of שבת. If so, the תורה could have just written 'Do not thresh while muzzling.' Why did it need to write the word 'ox'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the word 'ox' (שור) seems unnecessary. It asks what that word comes to teach.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We already include all animals through a גזירה שוה: 'ox' here and 'ox' in the שבת verse, which lists every animal. Since the word does not limit the law to oxen, it must be teaching something else. This sets up the next step.

steps.title: The worker and the animal are compared to each other
steps.stepSummary: The word 'ox' links the person who muzzles to the muzzled animal. Each one may eat from attached produce and from detached produce, just like the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: The word is there to compare the one who muzzles to the muzzled animal, and the muzzled animal to the one who muzzles. Just as the person eats from produce still attached to the ground, so may the animal. And just as the animal eats from produce already cut, so may the person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the word 'ox' creates a two-way comparison (היקש) between the worker and his animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On his own, the person was known to eat from attached produce, and the animal was known to eat from detached produce. The comparison passes each rule to the other side. Now both may eat from both kinds.

keyTerms.meaning: To compare, setting two things side by side in one law (היקש)

steps.whatToRemember: The word שור teaches a two-way היקש. The worker and his animal share their eating rights for both attached and detached produce.

steps.title: A worker eats only from things that grow from the ground
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא learns from the word 'threshing' (דיש) that a worker eats only from things that grow from the ground. This rules out milking and making butter or cheese.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: the verse says 'threshing.' What is special about threshing? It is done to something that grows from the ground, it is done when the work is being finished, and a worker may eat from it. So too, from anything that grows from the ground a worker may eat. This excludes someone who milks, makes butter, or makes cheese. Those do not grow from the ground, so a worker does not eat from them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that uses the word 'threshing' as a model. It limits the worker's right to eat to produce that grows from the ground.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Threshing has certain features, and the ברייתא carries over the main one: it is done to something that grows from the ground. Milk, butter and cheese come from animals, not from the ground. So workers making them may not eat from them.

steps.title: The vineyard verse already teaches this
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why we need the word 'threshing' for this rule. The verse about a neighbor's vineyard already limits eating to produce from the field.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need this? We already know it from 'When you come into your neighbor's vineyard.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא. Its lesson seems to be already known from another verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worker's right to eat comes from the vineyard verse, which speaks about growing produce. Milking and cheese-making do not happen in a vineyard, so they seem excluded already. That would make the word 'threshing' extra here.

steps.title: Without it, 'standing grain' might include everything
steps.stepSummary: The teaching is needed. Since the verse says 'standing grain' (קמה) to include every kind of standing produce, we might have stretched it to things that do not grow from the ground.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was needed. You might have thought: since the verse writes 'standing grain' to include everything that stands, maybe it also includes things that do not grow from the ground. So the ברייתא teaches us that it does not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the 'threshing' teaching blocks a mistaken idea. Otherwise the word 'standing grain' might have been read too broadly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word קמה was already used to widen the rule beyond the vineyard to all kinds of produce. Because it widens, we might have widened it even to animal products. The word דיש sets the limit: only things that grow from the ground.

keyTerms.meaning: It was needed

steps.whatToRemember: The vineyard verse gives the worker the right to eat, and קמה widens it to all produce. דיש puts a fence on it: only גידולי קרקע.

steps.title: A worker eats only at the finishing stage of the work
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא learns from 'threshing' that a worker eats only when he is doing the finishing stage of the work. This rules out a worker who weeds garlic and onions.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches about the word 'threshing.' Threshing is special because it happens when the work is being finished, and the worker eats then. So too, the worker eats from anything that is at the finishing stage of its work. This rules out someone weeding garlic and onions. That is not the finishing stage, so the worker may not eat from them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא that learns a different rule from the same word 'threshing.' It sets a time limit for when the worker may eat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Threshing is the last stage of preparing grain, so the ברייתא says eating is allowed only during finishing work like that. Weeding happens while the plants are still growing, so it is not finishing work and the worker may not eat.

keyTerms.meaning: The finishing stage of the work on the produce

steps.confusionAlert: This is a different lesson from the same word 'threshing' than the one in step 3. That step was about what kind of food the worker may eat. This step is about when he may eat it.

phrases.english: Another ברייתא teaches: 'Threshing'
phrases.notes: Same word from the פסוק about not muzzling an ox while it threshes (דברים 25:4).

steps.mimraCoreRuling: A worker eats only during the finishing stage of the work, so a weeder of garlic and onions does not eat.

steps.title: Why is this needed? The פסוק about the vessel already teaches it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why we need 'threshing' for this rule. The פסוק 'but into your vessel you shall not put' already shows the worker eats only at the stage of filling the owner's vessels.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need this? We can already learn it from 'but into your vessel you shall not put.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא. It says the rule about finishing work is already known from another פסוק, so the extra teaching from 'threshing' seems unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about the vessel shows that the worker eats when produce is being gathered into the owner's vessels. That is the finishing stage. So the lesson from 'threshing' seems to repeat what we already know.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need it? (a question that something is unnecessary)
It comes out from / is learned from
Your vessel

phrases.english: Why do I need this?

steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's lesson from 'threshing' about finishing work
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק about the vessel already limits eating to the finishing stage, so the extra teaching is not needed.

steps.title: Needed for a weeder who also pulls the small plants
steps.stepSummary: The teaching is needed for a weeder who also pulls the small garlic and onions from among the big ones. Even though those small ones are finished, he still may not eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for this case: even though he pulls the small ones out from among the thick ones, he still may not eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא teaches a new case that the פסוק about the vessel would not cover.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the weeder pulls out the small plants, that produce is in a sense finished and gathered. We might think the vessel פסוק would then let him eat. 'Threshing' teaches that he still may not, because the main work of the field is not finished.

steps.title: A worker eats only before the produce is finished for מעשר
steps.stepSummary: A third ברייתא learns from 'threshing' that a worker eats only from produce whose work is not yet finished for מעשר. This rules out a worker who separates dates and dried figs.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches about 'threshing.' Threshing is special because the grain's work is not yet finished for מעשר, and the worker eats from it. So too, the worker eats from anything whose work is not yet finished for מעשר. This rules out someone who separates dates and dried figs. Their work is already finished for מעשר, so the worker may not eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ברייתא with a different limit from 'threshing,' this time tied to the rules of מעשר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: While grain is being threshed, it is not yet obligated in מעשר. Dates and dried figs that are already gathered and stuck together are finished for מעשר. Separating them comes after that point, so the worker may not eat.

keyTerms.meaning: Its work is finished, so it now must have מעשר taken
One who separates (pulls apart stuck-together fruit)
Dates
Dried figs

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with step 6. There, eating is allowed only at the finishing stage. Here, eating is cut off once the produce is fully finished for מעשר. The worker eats in the window between the two.

phrases.english: so too anything whose work is not finished for מעשר,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a third ברייתא with yet another limit learned from 'threshing.'
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A worker eats only from produce not yet finished for מעשר, so a separator of dates and dried figs does not eat.

steps.title: A ברייתא says the separator of dates may eat
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says the opposite: one who separates dates and dried figs may eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a ברייתא teaches: one who separates dates and dried figs, a worker eats from it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא of step 9 with another ברייתא that seems to rule the opposite way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 9 says the separator of dates and figs may not eat. This other ברייתא says he may. The two sources seem to contradict each other.

phrases.english: But isn't it taught:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises a contradiction against the ruling of step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that a separator of dates and figs may not eat
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A different ברייתא directly says he may eat.

steps.title: רב פפא: that ברייתא is about unripe dates
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that the ברייתא allowing the worker to eat is talking about unripe dates. Their work is not yet finished, even after they are separated.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: When that ברייתא was taught, it was about unripe dates.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא resolves the contradiction. He shows the two ברייתות are talking about different kinds of dates.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unripe dates are picked early and left to finish ripening, so their work is not done for מעשר even after separating. The worker may eat from them. Ripe dates and figs are already finished, so the worker may not eat. This fits the rule of step 9.

keyTerms.meaning: When that ברייתא was taught
Unripe dates, picked early to ripen later

steps.whatToRemember: A worker eats only before the produce is finished for מעשר. Unripe dates are not finished yet, so a worker separating them may eat. Ripe dates and dried figs are finished, so he may not.

phrases.english: רב פפא said:
When that ברייתא was taught,

steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits the cases: the two ברייתות talk about different produce
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות argue about the same dates and figs.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא that allows eating is about unripe dates, which are not yet finished for מעשר.

steps.title: Another teaching from 'threshing': not yet finished for חלה
steps.stepSummary: A fourth ברייתא learns from 'threshing' that a worker eats only from food whose work is not finished for חלה. This rules out a kneader, a smoother and a baker.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches about 'threshing': threshing is special because the work on that grain is not yet finished for חלה, and a worker may eat from it. So too, a worker may eat from anything whose work is not yet finished for חלה. This rules out one who kneads, one who smooths the dough and one who bakes, because that dough is already finished for חלה, so the worker may not eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings one more ברייתא that learns from the word 'threshing.' This one uses חלה, not מעשר, as the cutoff point for when a worker may eat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Threshed grain is not yet at the stage where חלה must be taken. So the rule is: a worker may eat only until the food reaches the חלה stage. Once there is dough (kneading, smoothing, baking), the worker may no longer eat.

phrases.english: so too, any item whose work is not yet finished for חלה
a worker eats from it.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: A worker eats only from food not yet finished for חלה, so kneaders, smoothers and bakers may not eat.

steps.title: Isn't the dough already finished for מעשר?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why we need the חלה rule. By kneading time, the work was already finished for מעשר, and we already know a worker may not eat at that point.
steps.simpleTranslation: But isn't its work already finished for מעשר?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the new ברייתא. The kneader's dough passed the מעשר stage long ago, so we already know he cannot eat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא in step 9 already taught that a worker eats only before the work is finished for מעשר. Grain reaches that stage well before it becomes dough. So the חלה rule seems to add nothing new.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it so that (a challenging question)
The tithe taken from produce

phrases.english: But isn't its work already finished for מעשר!
phrases.notes: He means the step 9 ברייתא already rules this out, so why teach it again with חלה?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks step 12 as repeating something step 9 already taught.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for the חלה ברייתא in step 12.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Dough is past the מעשר stage, so the מעשר rule already forbids the worker to eat. The חלה rule is extra.

steps.title: Answer: the ברייתא is about חוצה לארץ
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the חלה ברייתא is about חוצה לארץ, where there is no מעשר. There, only חלה can be the cutoff point.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. We are dealing with חוצה לארץ, where there is no מעשר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to save the חלה ברייתא. It says the ברייתא is speaking about a place where the מעשר rule does not apply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If there is no מעשר, then the מעשר cutoff cannot be used. So we would need חלה to tell us when the worker stops eating.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult
Outside of ארץ ישראל
We are dealing with

phrases.english: It is not difficult: we are dealing with outside of the Land,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 13 by placing the ברייתא in a location with no מעשר.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case to a specific place
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The חלה ברייתא seemed to repeat the מעשר rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: In חוצה לארץ there is no מעשר, so חלה is needed as the cutoff.

steps.title: But there is no חלה there either
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the answer. In חוצה לארץ there is no חלה either, so the ברייתא could not be talking about there.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, there is no חלה either!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on its own answer. The place it picked also has no חלה, so the ברייתא can't mean that place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא's whole point is to use חלה as the cutoff. A place with no חלה obligation cannot be what it means. The answer from step 14 fails.

steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the ברייתא speaks about חוצה לארץ.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא built on חלה cannot speak about a place where there is no חלה.

steps.title: New answer: the 14 years of conquering and dividing the land
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא really is about ארץ ישראל, during the first 14 years. Then there was חלה but no מעשר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the ברייתא is really talking about ארץ ישראל, and it is not difficult. It speaks about the seven years they conquered the land and the seven years they divided it. As the Master said: in those seven years of conquering and seven years of dividing, they were obligated in חלה but not in מעשר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new answer. It finds a time when only חלה applied and מעשר did not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: During the first 14 years in ארץ ישראל, there was חלה but no מעשר. So the מעשר rule could not stop the worker, and the חלה rule was needed. This fixes the problem from step 15.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, actually
The seven years they conquered the land
The seven years they divided the land

phrases.english: Rather, it is really about the Land, and it is not difficult:
it is about the seven years they conquered and the seven years they divided,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר מָר: שֶׁבַע שֶׁכִּיבְּשׁוּ וְשֶׁבַע שֶׁחִילְּקוּ
phrases.english: as the Master said: in the seven years they conquered and the seven years they divided,
they were obligated in חלה but were not obligated in מעשר.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Drops the חוצה לארץ answer and gives a new answer to step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case to a specific time period
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא could not be about a place with no מעשר, since that place also has no חלה.
steps.terutzMaskana: In the 14 years of conquering and dividing, there was חלה but no מעשר, so חלה was the only cutoff.

steps.title: What matters is finished work, not the מעשר duty
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the 14-years answer. What stops the worker is that the work is finished, not whether מעשר must actually be taken.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it the מעשר that causes it? It is the finishing of the work that causes it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 16. Even in those 14 years, the grain still reached its finished stage, and that alone should stop the worker.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מעשר ברייתא used מעשר only as a sign of when the work is finished. The real reason the worker stops is that the work is done. That happens even when there is no מעשר duty, so the חלה rule is still not needed.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it really? (a challenging question)
Causes it, is the deciding factor
The finishing of the work

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the worker stops eating because of the מצוה of מעשר itself. מעשר is only a marker for the stage when the work is finished, and finished work is what really counts.

phrases.english: Is it the מעשר that causes it?
It is the finishing of the work that causes it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Knocks down the answer of step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the ברייתא is about the 14 years with no מעשר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The cutoff is finished work, which happens even without a מעשר duty. So the מעשר rule still covers the case, and the חלה rule is extra again.

steps.title: רבינא: join the two ברייתות into one teaching
steps.stepSummary: רבינא says the two ברייתות are really one teaching. Threshing is not finished for מעשר or for חלה, and a worker may eat from anything like that.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבינא said: combine them and teach them together. 'Threshing': just as threshing is special because its work is not yet finished for מעשר and for חלה, and a worker eats from it, so too a worker eats from anything whose work is not yet finished for מעשר and for חלה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא gives the final answer. The מעשר ברייתא and the חלה ברייתא are not two separate rules but one combined teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once they are joined, the חלה ברייתא is no longer a repeat. It is simply part of describing what threshing is: food not yet finished for מעשר or for חלה. The worker may eat until the food reaches its finished stage.

keyTerms.meaning: Combine and teach (join two teachings into one)

steps.whatToRemember: A worker may eat from produce only while its work is not yet finished, meaning before the מעשר stage and before the חלה stage. The two ברייתות are one teaching, so the חלה ברייתא does not repeat the מעשר ברייתא.
steps.whyThisMatters: This closes the series of teachings from 'threshing.' It shows that finished work is the real cutoff for a worker's eating, and מעשר and חלה are only the markers of that stage.

phrases.english: Rather, רבינא said: combine them and teach.
phrases.notes: Literally 'wrap and teach': join the two ברייתות into one teaching.

phrases.english: "Threshing": just as threshing is special
in that it is an item whose work is not yet finished
for מעשר and for חלה
and a worker eats from it,
so too, anything whose work is not yet finished
for מעשר and for חלה, a worker eats from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After both earlier answers fail, רבינא answers step 13 in a new way, by joining the two ברייתות.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading two sources as one combined teaching
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The חלה ברייתא seemed to be a separate rule that only repeats the מעשר rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is one teaching: threshing is not finished for מעשר or for חלה, and a worker may eat from anything like that.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A worker eats from produce only while its work is not yet finished for מעשר and for חלה.

steps.title: May a worker singe the produce in fire and eat it?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether a פועל may singe the produce in fire before eating it, or whether that counts like eating 'grapes and something else'.
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: may a worker singe the produce in fire and then eat it? Is that like eating grapes together with something else, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a brand-new question about a worker's right to eat. It asks whether he may roast or singe the produce a little in fire before eating it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the topic was when a worker may eat. Now the topic is how he may eat. Singeing makes the food tastier, which seems to add something beyond plain grapes. So the גמרא asks if this belongs to the case of 'grapes and something else'.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked before them (the חכמים); it opens an open question.
A hired worker, who may eat from the produce he works with.
That he singe, lightly roast.
Fire.
Grapes together with something else, used as the model for eating produce with an extra item.

phrases.english: A question was asked before them:
A worker: may he singe [the produce] in fire and eat it?
Is this like grapes and something else
or not?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after רבינא's answer about when the work is finished (Step 18).
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does singeing the produce in fire before eating it count like 'grapes and something else', or is it allowed?

steps.title: A proof from workers dipping bread in brine
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: a בעל הבית may give workers wine so they eat fewer grapes, and workers may dip their bread in brine so they eat more grapes.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: a homeowner may give the workers wine to drink so they will not eat many grapes. And the workers may dip their bread in brine so that they will eat many grapes!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer the question from Step 19 with a ברייתא. The ברייתא lets workers use brine so they will eat more grapes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא lets each side act in its own interest. The owner may cut down the workers' appetite with wine, and the workers may raise their appetite with salty brine. The גמרא wants to learn from this that a worker may do something to make his eating better or larger, so singeing should be allowed too.

keyTerms.meaning: The homeowner, the employer who owns the produce.
Is allowed, has the right.
To dip.
Brine, salty liquid that makes a person hungrier and thirstier.

phrases.english: Come and hear:

phrases.aramaic: רַשַּׁאי בַּעַל הַבַּיִת לְהַשְׁקוֹת פּוֹעֲלִים יַיִן
phrases.english: A homeowner is allowed to give the workers wine to drink
so that they will not eat many grapes,
and workers are allowed to dip their bread in brine
so that they will eat many grapes!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question asked in Step 19.
steps.raayaObject: That a worker may singe the produce in fire and eat it.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: workers may dip their bread in brine so that they will eat many grapes.
